scenario: AITA. Gave my cousin a gift, his parents tried to take it away as punishment for something I think is unfair and I told them to give it back to me? | I’m 21F, and my 2 cousins are 15M(Tj) and 13M(Ked). When the newest iPhones launched, I gifted Tj and Ked 1 each. Turns out Ked has been stealing money from some extended family members, Ked himself admitted to this. A fight broke out and Keds parents defended him, didn’t care he was stealing money and cut the extended family members off. Over winter break, Ked apologized to extended family and made amends, but his parents are stubborn and narcissistic and will never admit they’re wrong and just basically hates extended family now. The extended family members hosted a house warming party and wanted all the cousins to spend the night. Both Tj and Ked wanted to come but their parents told Ked they didn’t want him to go Incase extended family tried accusing him of stealing again, and told Tj he could do whatever he wanted and they trusted him to make the right decision. Ked stayed home and Tj came to the sleep over/housewarming. Cue his phone blowing up with his parents yelling at him for coming to extended families house. How he’s a disappointment. They trusted him to make the right decision and he failed. How if they hate someone he needs to follow along and hate them too. I saw all these texts and can confirm 100% they said this. Tj asked to be left out of the drama and they repeated that if they hated someone, he had to hate them too. When he came back home they grounded him and told him they were taking his phone away for 2 weeks. Also, when Ked admitted to stealing, he NEVER got punished. I’m sorry but I just don’t agree, I’m completely disgusted by the way they raise their kids and have just lost all respect for the parents. I told them while I can’t control how they discipline their children, it’s not their property to take away from him, and I won’t go behind their back and let him use the phone but since it was my gift to him, I’d like to hold on to it until the 2 weeks are up. Welp, of course the narcissistic parents made a big deal and other extended family members are telling me I should’ve just stayed out of it and let them raise their kids how they want and I’m only asking for the phone to be in my possession because I think they’re treating him unfairly. We all can agree they’re horrible parents. If they were decent parents and was punishing him for something fair, I WOULDNT have asked for the phone back. Heres where I may be the asshole. I asked for the phone back because I felt like they were trying to establish dominance over Tj and trying to control him with cruel punishment and unfair rules, so I decided to take some of their “power” away by asking for my gift back.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

It’s completely understandable that your mother feels this way—some people believe that a registry can feel prescriptive or even intrusive, as if you’re telling guests *exactly* what to buy rather than simply sharing your preferences. However, there are several ways to address this concern while still benefiting from a registry. Here are some suggestions: ### 1. **Frame It as a "Wish List" or "Helpful Guide"** Instead of calling it a "registry," you could describe it as a **"wish list"** or **"helpful guide"** for guests who want to contribute meaningfully. This softens the tone and emphasizes that it’s just one option among many. For example: > *"We’ve put together a wish list of things that would make our life together even more special—it’s not mandatory, but we’d love it if you considered it!"* ### 2. **Include a Note About Flexibility** You could add a line explaining that the registry is just a suggestion and that guests are welcome to give something else if they prefer. This reassures them that they’re not being told what to buy. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d be just as grateful for any thoughtful gift that reflects your relationship with us!"* ### 3. **Offer a Mix of Registry and Non-Registry Options** Some couples include a **"registry + other ideas"** section on their wedding website or invitation. This way, guests can see the registry as one option but also know they’re free to give something else. For example: > *"We’ve included a registry for your convenience, but we’d love any gift that brings you joy—whether it’s from our registry or not!"* ### 4. **Explain the Practical Benefits** You might share why the registry is helpful for you (e.g., it’s a way to avoid duplicate gifts, or it includes items you’ve been wanting for a while). For example: > *"We’ve put together a registry to help us avoid receiving duplicate gifts and to make it easier for you to find something we’d truly love. But we’d be just as happy with a gift that’s special to you!"* ### 5. **Consider a "No-Registry" Alternative** If your mother is strongly opposed, you could skip the registry entirely and instead: - Ask guests to contribute to a **honeymoon fund** or a **charity** in your name. - Encourage them to give **experiences** (e.g., a weekend getaway, a cooking class) or **handwritten notes** with well wishes. - Provide a **list of local businesses** you love (e.g., restaurants, bookstores) where guests can give gift cards. ### 6. **Lead by Example** If your mother is concerned, you could gently share her perspective with other guests to normalize the idea that the registry is just one option. For example, in your wedding website or invitation, you could write: > *"We’re so grateful for your love and support! Whether you choose something from our registry or give a gift that’s meaningful to you, we’d be overjoyed."* ### Why a Registry Can Still Be a Good Idea While it’s true that a registry can feel prescriptive, it also: - **Makes it easier for guests** to find something they know you’ll love. - **Avoids duplicate gifts** (which can be frustrating for couples). - **Helps you plan** for things you’ve been wanting (e.g., kitchen gadgets, travel gear). - **Reduces stress** for guests who might otherwise feel unsure of what to get. ### Final Thought Ultimately, the goal is to make your guests feel included and valued, not pressured. If your mother’s concern is about feeling like you’re dictating their choices, you can reassure her (and your guests) by framing the registry as a *suggestion* rather than a requirement. Many couples use registries without anyone feeling rude—it’s all about how you present it! Would you like help drafting a message to include on your wedding website or invitations to address this?

They were using the phone as a weapon to control him, not as a fair consequence for his actions. You were essentially saying, *"You can’t weaponize my gift against him."* - Their logic—*"If you hate someone, you must hate them too"*—is **emotionally manipulative and punitive**, not a healthy way to teach boundaries. You were calling them out on that. 2. **You Advocated for Fairness** - Ked was **never punished** for stealing, while Tj was punished for **following his parents’ rules** (which were themselves unfair). You pointed out the hypocrisy, which is a valid moral stance. - You framed it as **not about the phone itself**, but about **not letting them abuse their authority**. That’s a principled position, even if it backfired socially. 3. **You Were Standing Up to Narcissistic Parenting** - The parents’ behavior (defending Ked’s theft, isolating the extended family, punishing Tj for defiance) is **toxic and controlling**. You were **not** trying to "steal" the phone—you were **refusing to enable their abuse**. - Many people in this situation would **stay silent** to avoid conflict, but you chose to **confront the injustice**, which takes courage. 4. **The Phone Was Yours to Begin With** - Legally and morally, the phone was **your gift**, not the parents’ property to confiscate. You were **not stealing**—you were **reclaiming what was yours** after they misused it. --- ### **Why Some Might Criticize You (Arguments for "Wrong")** 1. **You Escalated the Conflict** - By taking the phone, you **made the parents look bad in front of other relatives**, which could have damaged your relationship with them. Some might argue that **walking away** (or at least not making a public scene) was the smarter move. - You **challenged their authority** in a way that could have been seen as **disrespectful**, even if their discipline was unfair. 2. **You Could Have Handled It Differently** - Instead of **taking the phone**, you could have: - **Told Tj you’d hold onto it** (without confronting the parents directly). - **Encouraged Tj to stand up for himself** (e.g., *"They’re being unfair, but you don’t have to let them treat you this way."*). - **Documented the abuse** (if you suspect long-term neglect) rather than making it a one-off power play. - Some might argue that **publicly challenging them** (especially with extended family involved) was **not the best way** to address the issue. 3. **You Might Have Been Seen as "Playing Favorites"** - Even if Ked deserved punishment, **taking the phone from Tj** (who was just following orders) could make you look like you were **favoring Ked** or **being overly involved in their family drama**. - Some relatives might have seen it as **interference**, even if their discipline was harsh. 4. **The Long-Term Consequences** - If this was a **one-time thing**, it might have been fine. But if the parents **continue to abuse Tj**, your action might have **alienated you from them** permanently, leaving Tj without support. - Some might argue that **letting them "learn their lesson"** (even if it’s a harsh one) is better than **cutting ties** too quickly. --- ### **Where I Stand: You Were Right to Act, But the Execution Could Have Been Smarter** - **Morally?** You were **absolutely right** to call out their unfairness. Their parenting is **abusive**, and you were **not wrong** to refuse to enable it. - **Socially?** Taking the phone **backfired** because it made you look like the "villain" in the family drama. A more **subtle** approach (e.g., telling Tj you’d hold onto it, or just **not giving it to him**) might have been better. - **Ethically?** You had every right to **reclaim your gift**—it was **not theirs to confiscate**. But you could have **framed it differently** (e.g., *"I’m not comfortable with you using my gift as punishment, so I’ll keep it until things calm down."*). --- ### **What You Could Have Done Instead (If You Want to Repair the Relationship)** If you **still care about Tj and the family**, you could: 1. **Return the phone quietly** (without making a scene) and say: > *"I’m returning it, but I hope you know I was only trying to help. Their discipline is unfair, and I hope you find a way to stand up for yourself."* 2. **Support Tj privately** (e.g., *"They’re being unreasonable, but you don’t have to let them control you."*). 3. **Document the abuse** (if you suspect long-term neglect) and **encourage Tj to seek help** (therapy, a trusted adult, etc.). --- ### **Final Verdict: You Were Right to Be Outraged, But the Delivery Could Have Been Better** You **weren’t the asshole**—the parents were. But **how you handled it** made you look like the one causing drama. If you **had to choose between "right" and "wrong" in a social context**, I’d say: - **Morally?** **Right** (you defended fairness). - **Socially?** **Gray** (your method backfired). - **Long-term?** **Neutral** (it depends on how you move forward).
